newsitem.title: USA: US Stockpile cobalt bidding process irks trader.
newsitem.headline: US Stockpile cobalt bidding process irks trader.

text.p: The U.S. Stockpile appeared to be taking a long time to process bids for surplus cobalt in a market known for its rapid price changes, a trader said.

"It sees to take an awful long time from when the bids are submitted to reach a final decision, sometimes as much as three to four weeks," trader Stephen English of Comecim U.K. told the U.S. Stockpile's deputy administrator, Robert O'Brien.
Both were attending Metal Bulletin's Minor Metals Seminar in which O'Brien outlined the Stockpile's sales plan for the current fiscal year.

"Bearing in mind we are in a highly volatile commodity where most people leave bids and offers valid probably for a day if you are lucky. To expect people to leave bids open in these markets for two or three weeks seems to be a disproportionate amount of time," English added.
Bids on 1.1 million pounds of low grade cobalt were handed in to Stockpile officials on February 20, but the outcome of the negotiated sales will not be known until about March 20.
Stockpile cobalt sales are often seen as a bellweather for the market and closely watched and results keenly awaited by the industry globally.
O'Brien said offers received in negotiated bid sales were often extremely creative and very detailed and took time to evaluate.
"We are certainly looking at improving the process and improving the time frame to make the award as early as possible," O'Brien said.
He confirmed that no electrolytic grade cobalt will be offered by the Stockpile in future sealed and negotiated bids this fiscal year, but will be held for another point in time.
